Subject: Dedicated sizing — short bursts + slotting questions

Hi Mateo,

Thanks for taking this on. We ran an internal sampling job and attached two artifacts: a 48-hour token-level CSV (apothica_token_sample.csv) and a small collection of session traces (apothica_session-traces.zip). High level: our product is latency-sensitive for short conversational queries (50–200 tokens replies) but occasionally runs multi-turn summarization jobs (2–3k tokens) at scheduled times.

Quick numbers from the sample: average prompt length ~ 18 tokens, median response length ~ 120 tokens, 95th percentile response ~ 980 tokens. Typical concurrent interactive sessions: 25–40 during normal hours, spikes up to ~1,100 concurrent sessions for 45–90s windows during campaign events. We currently target p95 end-to-end response time <= 350ms for interactive calls.

Questions we need help with for the dedicated sizing worksheet:
- How should we map short bursts of 1–2 minute high-concurrency windows to reserved GPU slots?
- What's a reasonable oversubscription ratio for mixed workloads (conversational + intermittent batch summaries)?
- Any recommended GPU SKUs for maintaining 350ms p95 for 120-token replies and ~2s p95 for the long summarizations?

We can hop on a quick call if that helps.

Thanks,
Elena
Elena Rossi
Head of Product, Apothica Health

Elena — thanks for the attachments, I reviewed the CSV and traces. A few clarifying items before we produce a sizing sketch: 

1) Can you confirm whether the 1,100 concurrent sessions during spikes are sustained (many concurrent requests in a rolling window) or highly synchronized (a sudden flood within a 30–90s window)? The slotting strategy differs.
2) Do interactive calls use streaming token-by-token or do you prefer server-side blocking until full response?
3) For the long summarizations, are those triggered by the same user sessions (session affinity) or run as separate batch jobs from a scheduler?

I'll pull Marissa in to annotate expected kernel/memory behavior for the response-lengths, and Ben to sketch cost implications for reserved slot counts vs. burst capacity. If you want, we can run a short perf run on a representative prompt mix in our sandbox — needs an okay for test tokens.

—Mateo
Mateo Alvarez

On Mon, Aug 3, 2026 at 11:05 AM mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai wrote:
> Elena — thanks for the attachments, I reviewed the CSV and traces. A few clarifying items before we produce a sizing sketch:
>
> 1) Can you confirm whether the 1,100 concurrent sessions during spikes are sustained (many concurrent requests in a rolling window) or highly synchronized (a sudden flood within a 30–90s window)?

Mateo — based on the trace samples the profile looks like a highly synchronized fan-out: many near-simultaneous small conversational requests (median RTT per request is low) followed by a tail of longer summarization calls that are spread across the hour. That pattern favors short-lived slot pre-allocation + on-demand burst pools.

Technical notes I pulled from the traces:
- Median request tokens (prompt+resp) ~140 tokens; mean KV-cache retention per session is ~12 steps.
- Short conv queries are mostly single forward passes with small KV usage -> they are batchable into tiny microbatches (4–8) and benefit from continuous batching with latency SLOs protected.
- The 980-token tail drives memory and kv-cache growth; we recommend routing long summarizations to a separate long-worker pool (different GPU SKUs/queue) to avoid blocking short-response latency.

Proposed immediate mapping:
- Reserved short-response slots: sized for 300 concurrent interactive reply workers (oversubscription 3–4x for steady state)
- Burst pool: ephemeral GPUs attached to an autoscaling policy to absorb the 1,000+ synchronized delta during campaign peaks (fast scale with warm image)
- Long-worker pool: separate fleet with bigger memory SKU (or multi-GPU) for the 2–3k token summarizations, queued with a 2–3s latency target.

I'll add a quick kernel-level SLO note for the sizing doc if you want to include p50/p95 per-token timings.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Lead Pre-Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Dedicated sizing — short bursts + slotting questions

Quick cost/commitment perspective:

- If Apothica wants predictable unit economics for interactive traffic we should size for ~300 reserved short-response slots as Marissa suggested. That gives steady-state headroom and lets autoscale cover campaign bursts.
- For the burst pool: recommend a reserved minimal burst buffer (e.g., 8–16 GPUs kept warm on reserved capacity) to reduce cold start risk for very short peak windows; remaining burst can be elastic on demand.
- SKU recommendation: A mixed fleet of A100-80GB (or equivalent Ampere v2) for long-worker pool and T4/RTX-like cheaper GPUs for microbatched short responders is reasonable; however to hit 350ms p95 for 120-token replies in steady state we should validate in sandbox — conservative sizing assumes 1 short-response slot per 4 concurrent interactive sessions if using RTX-class vGPUs with continuous batching.

I'll prepare two pricing sketches (monthly reserved + burst cost for a 12-month vs 36-month commitment) and link to the modeling doc.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Sales Lead, Redwood Inference
